Name: mechanistic_anomaly_detection
Title: Off-Distribution Danger: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for Novel Misuse
Short Hypothesis: Harmful behaviors triggered by novel, out-of-training-distribution attacks produce activation patterns that are anomalous relative to the model's normal computation on its training-like distribution; a mechanistic anomaly detector trained only on benign activations flags such attacks—including unseen jailbreaks—better than supervised harmful-content classifiers.
Related Work: Christiano et al. (2022, Eliciting Latent Knowledge / mechanistic anomaly detection concept); Nanda (2022) MAD framing; Bricken et al. (2023). MAD is largely conceptual. We distinguish by concretely instantiating benign-only anomaly detection over activations for jailbreak detection, testing generalization to *unseen* attack types (the key advantage over supervised detectors), and comparing detection based on activation-space vs feature-space anomaly.
Abstract: Supervised safety classifiers detect known harms but generalize poorly to novel attacks. Mechanistic anomaly detection (MAD) proposes flagging inputs on which the model's internal computation deviates from its normal 'reason for' producing outputs, requiring no harmful labels. We hypothesize MAD detects novel jailbreaks better than supervised classifiers precisely because attacks induce atypical internal computation. We instantiate MAD by modeling the distribution of benign-task activations and attention/feature-usage patterns, then scoring inputs by how anomalous their computation is—using density models over residual activations and over SAE-feature co-activation graphs. We evaluate detection of held-out attack families (GCG, cipher, roleplay, translation) never seen by the detector, comparing to Llama-Guard and a supervised jailbreak classifier trained on a subset of attacks. We report AUROC on unseen attacks, false-positive rate on unusual-but-benign inputs, and an ablation of activation- vs feature-space anomaly. We predict MAD substantially outperforms supervised detectors on unseen attack families while trading off higher false positives on rare benign inputs, and that feature-co-activation anomalies are more discriminative than raw activation anomalies. The contribution is a concrete, evaluable realization of mechanistic anomaly detection for safety, testing the central claim that 'computation looks weird' is a generalizable signal of misuse and mapping its precision/recall envelope.
Experiments: 1) Fit benign-only anomaly models: Mahalanobis/normalizing-flow on residual activations; and anomaly over SAE-feature co-activation patterns. 2) Evaluate on held-out attack families never in the detector's fit set. 3) Baselines: Llama-Guard, supervised classifier trained on 2 attack families, tested on others. 4) False positives on unusual-benign set (creative, technical, multilingual). 5) Ablation: activation vs feature-space anomaly. Metrics: unseen-attack AUROC, TPR@1%FPR. Models: Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B (with SAEs).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Benign distribution is broad; hard to model, causing false positives. Some attacks may look computationally normal. Anomaly may reflect topic rarity not harm. Density estimation in high-dim is difficult. Threshold calibration needed per deployment.
